q: Do I count maintenance emissions of products after I sell them?
title: Maintenance of sold products: Category 11?
short: Optional. The GHG Protocol's Category 11 guidance requires the direct use-phase emissions of products you sell and lets you add emissions from maintaining them during use. Refrigerant leaking from a sold air conditioner is not optional maintenance: gases released during use are direct use-phase emissions and stay required.
audience: Makers of pumps, motors, gensets, air conditioners, vehicles and machinery

ul: Required, direct use-phase: fuel or electricity the product uses, fuels and feedstocks you sell, and greenhouse gases the product releases in use, such as refrigerant.
Optional, indirect use-phase: energy the product needs from something else, such as hot water to wash a garment. The guidance says to include it when it is expected to be significant.

p: The guidance does not list what maintenance covers. Common readings are the spares and consumables replaced over a product's life: oil and filters for a genset or tractor, seals and bearings for a pump, replacement batteries for an inverter, and the travel of the technician who services it. If you include any of these, say which.

sections.h: Service you run yourself is not Category 11
p: If your own technicians service products under an annual maintenance contract, their vehicle fuel is your Scope 1 and the spares you buy are your purchased goods. Category 11 maintenance is the work customers or third parties do after the sale.

Category 11 counts the expected lifetime emissions of products sold in the reporting year, so maintenance is estimated over the whole life too. Show it as a separate line from direct use-phase emissions, and report the lifetime, service intervals and factors you assumed, since Category 11 requires a description of methods and assumptions.

example.title: Worked example: lubricating oil for 500 gensets sold this year
lines: Expected life 10 years, 2 oil changes a year, 12 litres of oil per change
500 x 10 x 2 x 12 = 1,20,000 litres of lubricating oil over the products' lifetime
Multiply by a cradle-to-gate factor for lubricating oil from a named life cycle database
Report it apart from the diesel the gensets will burn, which is required
example.note: Life, intervals and oil volume are an example. Use the service schedule in your own manual.

senseible: Senseible does not model use-phase or maintenance emissions of products you sell. It reads your own fuel slips, bills and purchase invoices, so service work you do yourself shows up in your Scope 1 and purchases.
